short: How far a soldier believes in you as her commander. It decides whether she obeys, refuses or walks away.
long: Trust runs from 0 to 100. It rises when you keep promises, protect her and decide in ways she respects; it falls when you lie, coerce her or leave people behind. When it drops, her [[loyalty_band|loyalty]] wavers. The Leash can force an order, but it costs Trust.

short: Personal warmth toward you, from cold to devoted. Unlike Trust it is about the person, not the rank.
long: Affinity runs from -100 to 100. It grows through kindness, shared time and being on her side, and sinks through insults, betrayals and coercion. Together with the other axes it decides which [[relationship_state|relationship state]] she can reach.

short: Romantic or physical interest, 0 to 100. It only grows while romance is switched on and she has reason to like you.
long: Attraction opens the romantic relationship states, but never forces them: a state also needs an event or a proposal. Switch romance off in the [[setting:romance|romance setting]] and it stays out of every reading and scene.

short: Strain on a soldier, 0 to 100. It sharpens her defects and, at the top, breaks her.
long: Fights, danger, refused orders and Leash use raise it; rest, calm company and the medbay lower it. It moves her through four bands: calm, strained, breaking and breakdown. Stress is not a relationship axis, but it changes how every defect plays.

short: From 50 Stress: the downsides of her defects bite harder and passives tied to Stress start to fire.
From 80 Stress: each turn she may lose control and act on her defect's breakdown instead of your orders.
At 100 Stress she breaks down: her defect's breakdown plays out until the expedition ends and she is released.
Out of the fight at 0 HP. Some skills can revive her; afterwards she is injured. A downed grunt may die, a named unit never does in combat.
Steady, wavering or breaking: how close she is to refusing orders or leaving.
long: It follows Trust with a delay, so it does not flicker: she turns wavering below 25 and breaking below 10, and recovers only at 35 and 20. Wavering units sometimes refuse orders; breaking ones may desert, and from the worst relationship states, mutiny.

short: Where your bond with a soldier stands: Stranger, Friend, Rival, Resentful and more. A state is entered through events, not numbers alone.
long: States unlock scenes, night visits, combat synergies and defect arcs, and they change how a soldier obeys and speaks. Axes and flags set the stage; an event or a proposal turns the page.

short: Six axes, from -3 to +3, that describe what a soldier cares about. They decide how she reacts to your decisions.
Results over principles. High: accepts ugly means for good ends. Low: refuses to cross lines.
Wants to choose for herself. High: bristles at orders and the Leash. Low: at ease being told what to do.
Loyalty to the squad. High: no one is left behind. Low: the mission comes first.
Compassion for the weak and the beaten. High: hates needless harm. Low: ruthless.
Faith in the corporation and its rules. High: follows the chain of command. Low: distrusts every contract.
Willingness to pay a price for others. High: gives herself first. Low: protects her own skin.
Your four social ranks, 1 to 5. They gate options and decide social rolls.
Making people follow. Used to talk a deserter down, press an order and hold a room.
Reading people and situations. Used to spot lies and hidden motives.
Understanding and comforting. Used to calm, reach and persuade through care.
Scheming and bargaining. Used for bluffs and clever deals; it also pays on contract work.
Money for upgrades, recruits, crafting and requisitions. Earned from contract work and missions.
Food, medicine and ammunition. Everyone eats every day; a shortage costs stress and goodwill.
Programmable polymer: the material for crafting and upgrading gear. Scarce, and needed for defect arcs.
The supplies the base eats each day: one per living soldier, reserve included, and one for you. A mess hall lowers it.
long: A day without enough supplies costs stress and Affinity across the squad, and after three days in a row it costs Trust too. Requisition more supplies with credits, or lower the bill with the mess hall.

short: Time comes in slots: morning, afternoon, evening and, only when something happens, night. Activities, talks and expeditions spend them.
You are hurt: training and work are blocked until you recover. Lovers and dependents may come to see you.
Command Points, your combat resource. Spend them on orders and ultimates; you gain one each round, up to five.
A corporate override you can request: Compel, Suppress or Terminate. Authorizations refill weekly, and every use costs relations.
long: Each request goes through an oversight form. Every use is logged, the squad notices, and soldiers who value their autonomy hate it. A soldier you use the Leash on may not forgive you.

short: Forces one order: in a scene her next reply complies, in combat it cancels a refusal. Costs Trust and Affinity and adds stress.
long: It spends one authorization. The target loses Trust and Affinity and gains stress; witnesses react according to their values, and repeated use can turn her resentful.

short: Stops a desertion or an attack in progress. Costs a lot of Trust and unsettles the whole squad.
Permanent deactivation. Needs a cause and an oversight approval, and the squad will not forget it.
A mandatory malfunction every soldier carries: an upside, a downside and a breakdown. It changes how she plays, not how strong she is.
A personal storyline about a defect: Cure, Manage or Embrace. It opens with trust, medbay level and time.
Removes the defect, upside included. She may feel like a stranger to herself.
Softens the downside and keeps the upside, but needs regular upkeep at the medbay.
Amplifies both upside and downside, and turns the breakdown into something the squad can use, or fear.
What her defect does at 100 Stress: she stops following orders and acts on the malfunction until released.
Hit points. At zero she is downed. Grows with level and gear.
long: Role base, plus growth per level, plus gear and percentage bonuses; each injury cuts it by a tenth, up to three injuries. Defects and statuses can change it for a fight.

short: Attack. It scales most of the damage she deals.
long: Damage is ATK times the skill multiplier, softened by the target's DEF. Weapons, affixes and some defects raise it, and effects that change damage dealt multiply the result.

short: Defense. It soaks part of every hit she takes.
long: Incoming damage is reduced by 100 divided by 100 plus DEF. Armor and some effects raise it; effects that change damage taken apply on top.

short: Speed. It decides who acts first each round.
long: Higher SPD acts earlier. Heavy armor lowers it by up to three; weapons can add or take away a point or two.

short: Critical chance, in percent. A critical hit deals one and a half times the damage.
Fights give experience; each level adds stats and one skill point. Your clearance caps how high she can go.
One per level. Spend them in her skill tree on actives, passives and upgrades. A respec costs PLYX and credits.
The skills she brings into a fight: four actives, plus her signature and ultimate. Change them on her sheet between fights.
Standard, refined, prototype, corporate or anomalous. Higher rarity means stronger stats and more affix slots; anomalous gear carries a drawback.
Craft, upgrade, reroll and dismantle gear. Each workshop activity opens a session with a few operations.
The four soldiers who go on expeditions. The rest wait in reserve; your barracks decide how many beds you have.
A generated soldier: ASCII portrait, Trust only, and mortal. Cheap to recruit, and a grunt who drops to zero HP can die.
A corporate access tier that raises the level cap. Story beats and base upgrades grant it: ten, twenty, thirty, then forty.
An unscouted spot on the expedition map. What it is shows only when you are near it or step in.
One choice in a decision. It tells you what it asks of you, never what it will change.
A small decision with modest stakes, often met on an expedition.
A weighty decision that can shift relations, resources or the world.
A rare decision the story will remember.
How hard the mission's fights are, 1 to 5. Higher danger means tougher enemies and better loot.
The class of payout for finishing the mission: credits, PLYX, loot and standing with the corporation all grow with the tier.
Days left to start the mission. When they run out the offer lapses, and some missions cost you when they do.
Missions on offer. Command and story missions stay posted; side jobs and rumor leads can be dismissed. Comms upgrades make the board bigger.
A mission run on a node map: you pick four soldiers, their rows and the supplies to carry, then walk the map. It spends the morning and the afternoon.
Overheard gossip from the base. Some rumors lead to a mission or a place worth scouting; the rest is atmosphere.
The connection profile of the mechanic model: it reads conversations and writes structured data.
How much the mechanic model may think before it answers. Minimal is cheapest; provider default leaves it alone.
With no mechanic profile set, use the main model for mechanic calls.
The smallest token limit sent on a mechanic call, so models that think have room to finish.
Expected output tokens per call type. Lower is cheaper; too low cuts answers short and forces a retry.
The most tokens the Alius context block may add to each main-model prompt.
The phosphor color of the Alius screen: amber, green or white.
Faint CRT scanlines over the screen.
A slight CRT flicker. Turn it off if it strains your eyes.
Shows model calls, prompts, content errors and the raw campaign state in the SYS tab.
Keeps mechanics view-only. Turn it off to edit the campaign state in the debug panel.
Allows Desire and Bond defects in imports and lists. A running campaign keeps the value it started with.
Shows exact numbers for relationships and stress instead of bands.
How a character's expression is chosen: by SillyTavern's own Expressions, or by the mechanic model.
A short generated vignette after an activity done with a companion (main model, one call each).
A generated name and one-line bio for newly recruited grunts.
When the mechanic model reads a conversation: after every exchange, every few exchanges, or only when the scene ends.
How many exchanges to wait between readings when the model reads every few exchanges.
Readings the model is less sure of than this are dropped.
After this many exchanges the scene header says time is passing.
How fast dialogue types out, in characters per second. Zero shows it at once.
Switches romantic states, Attraction and proposals on or off.
Old switch for explicit scenes. It is read once, to switch the 'Explicit scenes' category on in a campaign with no content choice yet. Categories decide now.
How often soldiers make romantic moves on their own: low, medium or high.
Lets soldiers start private messages with you on their own.
Condenses old chronicle lines with the mechanic model instead of just joining them.
Lets you rewind a lost combat and try again. The story does not remember rewinds.
Generated names for affixed enemies. Cached, and never holds up a fight.
Lets the mechanic model plan missions, rumors and story beats. Off: the engine's own fallback plans the world.
The minimum number of days between two story-beat proposals.
A narrative after-action recap written by the main model. The plain report always exists.
Lets the mechanic model write decisions. Off: the authored options of the template are shown.
Turns the analysis tool on or off: hover, press ? or long-press anything to read what it does.
How long the ANALYZING line plays: full (longer the first time), short, or off.
How long to hover before the analysis panel opens, in milliseconds.
Combat difficulty of this campaign: story, normal or hard. It scales enemy health, attack and defense.
How many days units take to stop judging the commander by looks. The first meeting counts most.
How hard the commander hits and how well the line holds. Shown as a word, never a number.
long: Strength helps when the commander has to push, lift or lean on someone, and it adds to an Authority talk-down together with experience. A weak commander is really weaker here; some checks stay closed, but every physical check has another way through. It grows by training, never by itself.

short: How much punishment and how many hours the commander can take. Shown as a word, never a number.
long: Endurance sets the commander's HP if a fight reaches the commander (Commander Crisis). With low endurance a long expedition exhausts the commander: the next morning is lost unless a close friend in the party covers. It grows by training.

short: How quickly the commander gets out of the way. Shown as a word, never a number.
long: Reflexes give the commander a chance to dodge a hit aimed at the commander in Commander Crisis. The better they are, the more often a blow misses. It grows by training.

short: How the commander presents, from very feminine to very masculine. It has no game bonus or penalty of its own.
long: Expression never buffs or weakens anything. It only matters through how each soldier reads it: individual tastes decide who notices, and the story may react to it. Nobody is punished for how they look.

short: The commander's visible experience, from green to veteran. It shapes first impressions and the weight of a word.
long: Seasoning is how much the commander has clearly lived through. It adds to presence on first meeting and, together with Strength, to an Authority talk-down. Scars from a lost Crisis fight can raise it.

short: The commander's physique in one word, from frail to hardened, worked out from the three body stats.
long: Frail, slight, average, fit or hardened. The build decides which presence action the commander gets in a fight and which acts the squad finds out of character: a gentle commander who coerces, or a tough one who comforts, makes a bigger impression until they know each other better.

short: A slight commander's once-per-fight trick: enemies look past the commander about half of the time.
long: Free, once per combat. For the rest of the fight an enemy that could pick the exposed commander skips the commander on about half of its decisions. It does nothing if the commander is not exposed.

short: An average commander's once-per-fight trick: the next order costs 1 CP less.
long: Free, once per combat. The next order you pay for costs 1 CP less, and can cost nothing. Free orders and repeats do not use it up.

short: A fit commander's once-per-fight trick: every standing soldier loses 10 stress at once.
long: Free, once per combat. Every soldier still on her feet gets 10 stress relief, which her own traits may change. It needs no exposed commander.

short: A hard task has more than one way: your body, a soldier's help, your rank, a tool or a price.
long: Some choices ask how you get it done. A body route needs a physical stat, but there is always another way through: ask a soldier, use your rank, an item, or pay. A weak commander is really weaker, never stuck.

short: Someone else does it for you. She agrees if she trusts you enough, and it costs her warmth and stress.
long: The soldier you ask answers by her Trust in you. Enough Trust and she does it, perhaps with a remark. Less than that, or a breaking loyalty, and she refuses. Only an agreement is paid for.

short: An insomniac commander is awake with nobody at the door. Sleep, or spend the night and pay for it tomorrow.
long: When no one knocks, a commander who cannot sleep gets the Night slot anyway. You can SLEEP it away at no cost, or do an evening activity; a night spent awake lowers the Empathy rank by one the next day.

short: How the commander comes across at a first meeting: build, experience and the weight of Authority.
long: Presence moves a soldier's Trust once, the day she joins, scaled by her tastes. It matters most on first meeting and fades as she gets to know the commander; what the commander does matters more and more. It is never shown as a number unless raw values are on.

short: Looks count most the day a soldier meets the commander and fade with every day she knows the commander.
long: A unit's first impression decays over days (the setting First impression fades). While it lasts, acts that do not fit the commander's build land harder, and the narration is told that the squad is still sizing the commander up.

short: A commander who acts against the picture the build gives makes a bigger impression, for better or worse, until the squad knows the commander better.
long: A gentle commander who coerces, or a hard one who comforts, shocks. The effect is strongest at first and fades with the days a unit has known the commander. Some soldiers' tastes make it stronger. The engine tags the act, never the model.

short: Up to two regular traits and one special one change how the commander plays, not how strong the commander is.
long: Every trait has an upside and a downside. Regular traits shape growth, costs and first impressions; a special trait can reshape the campaign. Picked when the file is made; there is no way to change them later.

short: A weak commander loses the next morning after a three-slot expedition, unless a close friend in the party covers.
long: Endurance 2 or less. The squad comes back, the commander sleeps through the morning and the day starts in the afternoon. A unit that is a friend or closer, in the party and standing, takes the strain instead.

short: How hard the defective soldiers are to win and to keep: how fast Trust is gained and lost, and how often they refuse, desert or mutiny.
long: The world sets a level from kind to hazardous. It changes how fast Trust and Affinity are won and lost, how easily loyalty breaks, how long a relationship waits before it moves on, how likely refusals and desertions are, and who a breakdown turns on. It changes none of a soldier's combat stats. Each named soldier may sit up to two levels away from the world's level; grunts follow the world.

short: How far one soldier sits from the world's disposition, from two steps kinder to two steps harder, proposed from her character card.
long: The offset is proposed when the card is imported, with a one-line reason, and you can change it. A soldier two steps kinder than a hazardous world reads as a prickly one. The offset moves only her own rules, never another soldier's.

short: Whether a soldier shares, ignores or rejects one of the world's norms. A norm reaches the squad only through each soldier's own stance.
long: Stances are proposed from the character card and can be edited. A soldier who shares a norm starts colder toward a commander who breaks it and warms up as the days pass; one who rejects it may like the commander better for breaking it. Strength 2 is a stronger stance. A stance does nothing while the world's setting for that norm is neutral.

short: The options chosen before the campaign: prejudices, oversight, tone and the disposition of the squad. Most are fixed when the campaign starts.
long: The world's options are written into the campaign when it starts and cannot be changed afterwards, except those marked as changeable (how graphic the Bloom is described). Their short lore lines are part of what the story model is told on every reply.

short: How safe a soldier feels defying the commander: what she expects to happen to her if she does. It is not Trust.
long: Trust asks whether she believes in the commander's orders; Impunity asks what it costs her to ignore them. It grows when defiance goes unanswered, when threats are not carried out, when the Leash looks like a bluff and when the rest of the squad grows bold. It shrinks when the commander follows through, when she needs the commander, and when the commander's presence holds her back. The game shows it in words: cowed, low, high or brazen.

short: How a soldier relates to the commander's authority, from Trust and Impunity: disciplined, defiant but loyal, fearful, openly defiant or indifferent.
long: High Trust with low Impunity: she obeys by the book and objects on the record. High Trust with high Impunity: she argues, does it her own way and will not abandon the commander. Low Trust with low Impunity: she complies in silence, sabotages quietly and would run rather than fight. Low Trust with high Impunity: she mocks, makes demands, ignores orders and may mutiny. Middling Trust and Impunity: she does not much care who commands her, and simply does what is asked. The stance shapes how she refuses an order, how often she makes demands and what she does when she breaks.

short: The part of Impunity that remembers: defiance nobody answered raises it, a carried-out punishment lowers it, and it fades by a point a day.
long: Each soldier keeps her own record. Letting a defiance pass, backing down from a threat or giving way raises it; imposing a consequence, or the Leash, lowers it. Every day it moves one step back toward nothing. The squad's mood adds a little of the others' records to hers.

short: A secret a soldier holds over the commander, such as the crime she learned about. Each one makes her feel safer defying the commander.
long: A secret counts only while someone else in the squad does not share it. Once everybody knows, it is no leverage at all.

short: A consequence the commander warned of but did not impose. If it is not carried out by the end of the next day, the squad sees the commander back down.
long: The game shows whether she believes the threat. Carrying it out, or using the Leash, keeps it. Letting it lapse counts as backing down and raises her Impunity.

short: A fearful soldier's quiet protest: missing supplies or credits, or a faulty pack on the next run. Nobody sees who did it.
long: A soldier who is afraid of the commander and cannot say no may say yes and undermine the order instead. The loss is small and the game never names who was behind it.

short: The commander's consequences below the Leash: a reprimand, revoked rations or leave, extra duty, a bench, the brig. They cost relations and lower her Impunity.
long: Pick a measure from the DISCIPLINE menu, or say it in the conversation and the game reads it. A soldier takes it harder when it touches something she cares about. A threat that is never carried out counts as backing down.

short: The game read a punishment in your words and applied it. If it misunderstood, UNDO puts back exactly what it changed.
long: A chip appears whenever the game registers a punishment or a threat, whatever the display settings say. UNDO is offered on the same day and, in a scene, while the scene is open; it leaves no memory of the moment.

short: What a punishment keeps a soldier from for a while: the brig, no leave, a bench for the next expedition or a slot of extra duty.
long: The brig keeps her out of scenes, companions and expeditions. No leave keeps her from being anyone's companion except for talking and the medbay. A bench leaves her out of the next expedition. Extra duty covers one slot.

short: Something a soldier asks of the commander: more food, a room, to be left out of a run, a weapon. Grant it, refuse it or talk it over.
long: A soldier who feels safe asking will ask. Granting costs something and buys goodwill; refusing costs relations, more so with a soldier who feels safe, and may turn into open defiance. A demand left unanswered for two days counts as a refusal. TALK opens a conversation and keeps the demand open.

short: The price of a favor a soldier did while she was not yet willing. She will want something for it, and refusing breaks a promise.
long: When the commander asks a soldier who trusts a little less than the task needs, she may do it anyway and bill later. Refusing what she then asks counts as breaking a promise.

short: What the squad has learned to say about the commander from what the commander does, kept as nicknames.
long: The game counts deeds: Leash requests, conscripts lost, defiance let pass, punishments, demands granted or refused. When a pattern is clear enough, one soldier says the nickname aloud for the first time, and from then on it is on the commander file. Up to two are held at once, one per kind; a nickname that stops being earned fades after a week, and a stronger pattern of its kind takes its place. A nickname shifts how bold soldiers feel and how soldiers with certain values think of the commander.

short: A name the squad gives the commander once a pattern of deeds is clear. It is said aloud first in a private scene.
long: Nicknames come from deeds, not from choices on a menu. The first one waits for a quiet moment with one soldier; a group scene never introduces it. It is then public: every soldier knows it, and the commander line the main model reads carries it. Some soldiers like what it says about the commander and some do not. Each soldier's Trust moves once, by her own values.

short: Lets the mechanic model put a soldier's demand into her own words. Off, the written text is used as it is.
long: Costs one short model call per demand. The rules decide what she asks for; the model only chooses the words.

short: The outpost seen as a cross-section: its rooms, who is in them right now, and what needs you today.
long: The hub is the home screen. Each room shows the soldiers who are there this slot. Tap a room to see who is present, talk to someone or start an activity. Open the [[pda_device|PDA]] for the full tabs. [[whereabouts|Where soldiers are]] can change every slot.

short: Where a soldier is this slot. It follows her injuries, orders and tastes, and can change when the slot or the day does.
long: Nobody keeps a timetable. Where a soldier is comes from what the outpost knows: the injured lie in the medbay, a confined soldier stays in quarters, a soldier on duty works her shift, and at night everyone sleeps. Otherwise she drifts to rooms that are open and that she likes. Reopening the screen never moves her; only a new slot or day does.

short: The ring and symbol on a soldier's marker: ! danger, ♥ bond, + trust, * affinity, ~ warning, · nothing notable.
long: The ring color is always paired with a symbol, so it never has to be read by color alone. ! means stress is high, she is injured or her loyalty is breaking. ♥ is a romantic bond. + is a trusting friendship. * is strong personal warmth. ~ means a cold relationship or rising stress. The state glyph beside it names her [[relationship_state|relationship state]].

short: What the outpost is working toward right now: the current prologue step, the story, a lead from the director, or a soldier who wants to talk.
long: The hub shows one standing order. During the [[prologue]] it is the current step. Afterwards a story beat that is ready comes first, then the director's latest lead, then soldiers waiting on an answer. With nothing to follow it falls back to the mission with the nearest deadline, and reads NO STANDING ORDERS when there is none.

short: What is waiting for you by the end of the day: knocks at the door, unread messages, answers owed and deadlines.
long: The list shows only what you could already learn from the PDA. It never reveals what a soldier is hiding. A mission due today or tomorrow, a shortage or an injury may also appear here.

short: Pass the current slot without doing anything. The time is spent and nothing is gained.
long: Use it when there is nothing worth doing. It costs the slot like any other action, and the day moves on when the last slot is gone. A quiet night is spent asleep instead. It is blocked while a conversation, an expedition, a decision or a late visitor is waiting.

short: Your handheld. It slides up over the hub and holds every tab; its casing follows your corporation.
long: Press Tab, or the OPEN PDA button, to raise it, and Tab or Esc to lower it. Number keys 1 to 8 open a tab directly. The casing is only a skin: it changes nothing in the game, and you can pick another in SYS.

short: Out on an expedition. A soldier who is away is in no room and cannot be talked to until the squad returns.
long: The AWAY strip lists the party of an open expedition. They are back on the hub when it ends.

short: The casing of your PDA. It follows your corporation unless you pick another here. It changes nothing in the game.
long: Each corporation issues its own handset: standard CCP surplus, Kestrel-Ward steel or Vesper ceramic. Leave this on the campaign's own to follow your corporation, or pick any casing you like. The screen inside looks the same in every one.

short: Switches off scanlines, flicker, dithered portraits and the tab glitch, and makes the text larger.
long: Use it when the terminal look gets in the way of reading. Colors and layout stay as they are. It does not stop slides and fades: for those use Reduce motion.

short: Nothing slides, fades, boots or types out. It also follows the system's reduced-motion setting.
long: With it on the PDA appears at once, the boot is skipped, replies show in full and the oversight review does not play out. The analysis panel shows its text without the ANALYZING line.

short: Five tones for rings, pips and bars: danger, bond, trust, affinity and warning. A symbol always goes with the color.
long: ! danger, ♥ bond, + trust, * affinity, ~ warning. The tones differ in brightness as well as hue, so they can be told apart without color vision. Nothing is ever shown by color alone.

short: PDA portraits are redrawn in the three tones of your phosphor palette. Scenes keep full color.
long: The portrait is turned into a pattern of dots in the screen's own colors, like an old terminal image. It is switched off by Readable mode.

short: How loud the PDA's small sounds are, 0 to 100. The default is low.
long: Covers the device, tab and notification sounds, the typing ticks, the stamp and the ambient hum. Nothing plays until you do something that makes a sound.

short: Silences every sound of the extension without changing the volume.
A very low engine hum that plays while the shell is open. Off by default.
long: It follows the volume and the mute setting and stops when you close the shell.

short: The opening of a new campaign: intake, medical exam and dossier, a line-up with the squad, a short patrol and a first evening.
long: Everything before the first free day is guided. Each stage has a [[objective]] on the hub, and the PDA tabs open one by one. A repeat player can take the [[veteran_intake]] and skip the patrol.

short: The clerk asks for the article of the conviction and a name for the record.
long: The article decides the commander's crime and perk; the name is how soldiers will address the commander. Both can be changed on the dossier before signing.

short: The medic dictates what the examination finds: build, how the commander presents, and notes for the file.
long: Build is the three body stats, presentation is the expression, and notes are the commander traits you choose. The wording on each line comes from the numbers.

short: The commander's whole file. Review it, change what you like, then sign to deploy.
The classic setup form instead of the in-world intake, and no tutorial patrol.
long: It fills in the same commander fields as the intake, medical exam and dossier, just as plain forms. The line-up and first words still happen.

short: The first meeting with the whole squad. It runs about six exchanges, then offers to move on.
long: You can keep talking or end it. The line-up never uses up a slot.

short: A short private exchange with each soldier, two or three replies each.
long: You can skip any soldier. It never uses up a slot.

short: A short authored expedition: one fight, one decision, the objective. It teaches the combat and expedition screens.
long: A lost or abandoned patrol does not block the story. Combats in it can always be retried; stress and injuries still count.

short: A PDA tab that has not come online yet.
long: Tabs open on a day or after a story step, with a notice when they do. LOG and SYS are always open.

short: A one-line tip that appears at the top of a screen during the shakedown patrol.
long: Press GOT IT to dismiss it. Focus anything and press ? for more.

short: Each side stands in a front or a back row, three to a row.
long: Melee skills hit only the front row while anyone stands in it; ranged skills reach either row. Set the formation before an expedition.

short: How a soldier leads, attaches and what she will not do, read from her character card.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The bond profile has her lead style (who takes the lead in close moments), her attachment (how fast and how hard she attaches), her desire, whether she is a caretaker, how open she wants a relationship to be and a list of things she will not take part in. A soldier with a modest profile never uses the romance mechanics beyond conversation. Her own limits hold even when a content category is switched on.

short: What the story may show. Every category is off until you switch it on; switching one on is your consent for it to appear when the story leads there.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Categories are listed when you start a campaign and in the settings tab, and you can change them at any time. A category that is off is excluded from every generation and from every mechanic that could produce it; when a reply shows one anyway it is marked and you can regenerate it. A soldier's own limits from her card still hold when a category is on.

short: A category that only makes sense with another one. It cannot be switched on while the other is off, and it goes off with it.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Some categories build on another (watersports on bodily fluids). The toggle shows what it needs and stays locked until that one is on; switching the needed one off switches this one off too.

short: A point of tension in a scene with three ways to answer. The game decides when it comes and what each answer is; the words are written for the scene.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A moment comes when something in the scene tips: she asks, someone is at the door, a limit is near. There are always three answers: give way, hold out, or turn it. The labels are written to fit the scene, and you may type your own answer instead.

short: The body side of a close contact: a gauge that drains or fills, and a way to play it. It runs in short segments that do not wait for the story.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Some contacts carry a gauge (air, strength, saturation, cleanliness, her task, the jaw). It runs in segments, one beat at a time or in real time, and the story only reports it. The stop word ends it at once, whatever she wants.

short: How well the commander's body takes a hold. It grows with each hold endured and with drills, and it widens the gauge.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Endurance is kept per kind of hold: breath, weight, jaw. It rises by 10 for a hold endured, by 2 for each window caught after three in a row, and by 15 for a drill on TRAIN once a day. A weaker body endures less.

short: A state the commander is in for a while, such as dizzy after a blackout or stiff after a long hold.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A condition lasts until the day ends or until the next slot. Dizzy lowers social rank and adds stress; stiff only shapes the story.

short: A scent, a sweat or a taste the commander meets in a contact. The body gets used to it, then seeks it, and the story words it as perception.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Each kind has a tolerance that grows with exposure and slips back apart, a reflex when it is too strong, and a trajectory from aversion to adoring. The story describes what is perceived, never what the commander feels.

short: Who is where in the scene: posture, place, contact, what is worn and what each person is doing. The game keeps it and tells the story every turn.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The blocking is the shape of the scene. Each person has a posture, a place, perhaps a contact with someone, things they wear and something they are doing. You set it with the chips under the chat, the story reports changes, and the game checks every one. Anything not set stays out of the story.

short: A part of her, or something of hers, that the commander may be asked to worship: feet, hands, hair, boots and so on. Each is a content category toggle.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Targets are on a body map and each has its own scent and taste. Whether a target appears at all depends on the content categories you have switched on and on her own limits.

short: How she answers when an answer is not the one she expected: a nudge, a look, a pull. The game picks the kind from what is in the scene.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: When your answer is the opposite of what she expected, she may escalate. The kind follows the scene: a pull on the lead, a press, a nudge with her foot, a look. The story writes the act.

short: Busy hands or a covered face: the PDA cannot be used, and every tab is locked until the contact or the item is gone.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Some items and contacts leave no hand free for the device (paw mitts, a smothering hold). While one is in place the tabs are locked and only the scene chat works. The lock lifts as soon as it ends; tabs the opening days keep locked stay locked.

short: Who is where, in what posture, touching whom and wearing what. The chips set it; the story must follow it.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The strip under the transcript shows one row per person. A chip can be examined for what it does. The movement buttons change the commander's posture, and [ + ] adds a place, a contact or an item the scene allows. A button that is grayed out shows why. Changes made after a reply are taken back if that reply is swiped.

short: Who drives a romantic scene: the soldier, the commander or both. The game decides it from her style, her Impunity and what happened lately.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: When a scene turns romantic the game decides who leads it and tells the story so. A soldier who leads sets the pace and may ask for things; one who follows waits for the commander. You can follow her lead (a small warm gesture), ask what she wants, or set a boundary for this scene. Boundaries are in the fiction; they are not the content categories.

short: How strongly a soldier wants the commander, built up day by day. It shows as a word; unmet, it makes her restless, then irritable, then it breaks her.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Want only runs for soldiers whose card gives them a real desire and who are close to the commander. It grows each day, and falls when the two spend time together, when she trains beside the commander, when a night together happens or when a dangerous run takes her mind off it. From a point she starts writing first and may come to the door; later she is on edge; at the top her defect may break her for a day. She asks for it herself: you can satisfy, postpone or talk.

short: A soldier who leads in a close bond may ask the commander to live by a rule. Accept it, negotiate a version, or refuse; a broken rule costs trust and warmth.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A leading partner proposes a rule in her own words, in the scene or as a message. Accepting makes it binding: some rules the game checks itself (a day without contact, a run taken without her), others it reads from what you say and do. A broken rule lowers her Trust and Affinity and stresses her, and others who saw it remember. You can negotiate: you talk it through and agree a version both can keep. She asks for no more than three at a time, and none that you have switched off.

short: The mechanic model puts a soldier's rule proposal into her own words. Off, the proposal uses the template text as it is.
The mechanic model puts the one-line reason behind each soldier's ballot in a squad vote into words. Off, the reason uses the template line of the vote.
The mechanic model words the edit a soldier with access to your messages makes before one goes out. Off, an authored line is used.
How open a romantic relationship is: secret, known to those close, or public. She has her own preference; you choose the level.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Publicity only exists while a soldier is in a romantic relationship with the commander. A relationship starts at the more private of her preference and known. You can change it any time: moving toward what she prefers is heard, moving away is dismissed. A secret can come out when others are around, and a mismatch makes her ask to talk. Going public while she leads makes the rest of the squad react by what they value.

short: How hard the squad pushes for itself: leader privileges, how often soldiers make demands, and how much the commander's vote weighs.
long: A world option fixed at the start. Low trims a leader's privileges by a quarter and trims demands; high raises both by half and a quarter, and when the squad [[voting|votes]] each soldier's vote counts a quarter more and the commander's a quarter less. It only scales what the soldiers' own character already does: a yielding soldier never turns dominant because of it.

short: With squad votes on, some of the commander's decisions go to the squad first: they vote for or against the commander's pick.
long: A world option fixed at the start, off by default. When it is on, a mission from the board, a base upgrade, a mild punishment, a ration choice in a shortage and a scapegoat decision open a vote. The commander picks first and always votes for the pick; each soldier's ballot follows her values, her trust in the commander and what the decision does to her. A tie goes to the commander. A failed vote can be accepted, or overruled at a price.

short: The squad's vote on a decision of the commander: each soldier votes for or against the commander's pick. A tie goes to the commander.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: With squad votes on, a mission from the board, a base upgrade, a ration mode in a shortage, a mild punishment and who takes the blame open a vote. The commander picks, always votes for the pick, and weighs more with Authority. Each soldier's ballot follows her values, her trust, her stance toward the commander, an open demand and what the decision does to her. A failed vote can be accepted, or overruled by an order, a punishment or the Leash: that costs Trust and raises Impunity with everyone who voted against.

short: How a shortage is shared out: evenly, fighters first (the reserve goes without), or the commander going without first.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: While supplies cover the day's upkeep the mode changes nothing. In a shortage, Equal spreads the missing supplies over everyone. Fighters first lets the reserve soldiers go without before the active roster feels it. Commander short lets the commander go without, up to the commander's own share, at the cost of sleeping through the next morning. While the world has squad votes on, a change of mode in a shortage goes to a [[vote]].

short: How much weight a soldier carries in the squad: her recent fights, how well the others get on with her and how safe she feels defying the commander.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Standing is worked out for every named soldier and refreshed weekly. Merit counts damage dealt, finishing blows and healing from the last 14 days. Respect is how alike her values are to the others'. Impunity is how safe she feels defying the commander. Her lead style then multiplies it: a dominant soldier counts 30 % more, a yielding one 30 % less. The soldier far enough ahead of the next, and whose card says she pushes for power, becomes the [[squad_leader]].

short: The soldier the squad looks to. She is far enough ahead in standing and her card says she pushes for power. Her vote weighs more and outsiders address her.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A leader appears only when one soldier leads the next by a clear margin and her card says she pushes for power; a balanced or yielding soldier never becomes one. She votes with more weight, the squad's grunts follow her vote, her record of defiance rubs off on the others more and she may [[countermand]] a minor order. You can [[endorse]] her or [[challenge]] her. Outsiders address her as the one who runs the unit ([[outside_perception]]).

short: The squad leader overrides a minor order you gave to another soldier. You can accept it, or overrule her at a price.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Only a minor order that names another soldier can be countermanded: training, rest, work or study. When it happens nothing of the order is done and no slot is spent. Accepting drops it. Overruling runs the order anyway, costs the leader Trust and raises your Impunity with her. A countermand not answered lapses with the slot.

short: Make the squad leader your formal second-in-command: her privileges grow by half and outsiders treat her as such.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Endorsing raises her Trust and Affinity, raises every other soldier's Impunity a little, makes her privileges half as large again and makes it the official arrangement for outsiders, who then address both of you. It ends when she stops leading.

short: Contest the squad leader's place on one stat. One roll decides it; either way the next challenge waits two weeks.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Pick authority, empathy, strength, endurance or reflexes. The odds depend on your rank in that stat against hers. Winning removes her leadership for two weeks; losing raises her standing for two weeks and everyone's Impunity. You need no open scene, and the result opens a scene with her.

short: Outsiders (oversight, traders, enemy commanders) address the squad leader as the one who really runs the unit, until you show otherwise.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: While a leader exists, oversight copies her on messages and outsiders address her. A visible feat holds that back for two weeks: surviving a crisis with cover, securing a command mission after giving an order, or settling a decision by a passed social check. Endorsing her makes it the official arrangement and it is never held back. Only the directive and oversight's copy are built; trading and parleys have no system yet.

short: When a decision the squad took ends in a failure oversight punishes, you answer for it or shift it onto the soldier who carried the vote.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: After a command mission the squad voted for fails, oversight wants a name. Take the blame and oversight punishes the commander: standing with the corporation falls and a Leash authorization is lost, but the soldier who carried the vote and those who backed her trust the commander more. Shift it and oversight confines her for two days and strains her, and the squad turns against the commander, her most of all.

short: A soldier with a will of her own sometimes takes a decision in the field herself. A bad one marks the run: if it fails, oversight wants a name.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: At an event on a run, a soldier who pushes for power, or who defies the commander openly, may decide for the squad without asking. The engine picks who and how it turns out, from her values and her Impunity; nobody rolls and nothing is offered to choose. A good call earns her merit and boldness and blames nobody. A bad call costs the run (supplies, stress, wounds) and marks a command mission: if the run later fails, oversight asks for a name and the commander answers for her or shifts it onto her. The ASK ME FIRST order stops it for one soldier.

short: A standing order: she must ask before deciding anything in the field. Giving it costs her Trust; it holds until it is lifted.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: While the order holds she never takes a decision on her own at an event, however bold she is. Giving it goes against her values and costs Trust once, like an overruled decision; lifting it is free. It can only be given or lifted at the base, and a run that is under way reads it live at every node.

short: How far a soldier reaches into the commander's PDA: decor (1), notes (2), calendar (3), messages (4). It grows with closeness and boldness.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A soldier with an imported profile who is close enough, or bold enough, leaves her mark on the device: stickers, her picture, a renamed contact. Higher up she pins notes and the rules she has set, books time on the calendar and, at the top, edits an outgoing message or stops a request before it goes out. Each level allows only its own thing. Peeling decor costs her Affinity; undoing an edit counts as defiance. When her access falls, her decor stays as a faded mark for a week.

short: A soldier with calendar access books a slot of the commander's time. At that slot the commander goes to her, or cancels, which counts as refusing a demand.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: She books tomorrow's evening or afternoon and tells the commander in a message. While the booked slot is under way and she can be met, nothing else can use it: go to her, or cancel. Canceling costs Trust, Affinity and stress like a refused demand, and more when she does not fear the commander's reaction. Two bookings of one slot clash: choose one, or let the two settle it by how hard each holds on. A booking she cannot keep (the brig, an injury, a run) lapses at no cost.

short: A soldier who leads takes the initiative: she writes and knocks twice as often and may propose the next step herself.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Only a soldier with an imported profile who takes the lead and is in, or close to, a romantic step courts. Deflecting closes her proposal at no cost. A condition is a short sentence that becomes her promise: she holds the commander to it. She may also claim the commander in public.

short: She has made it plain to everyone that the commander is hers. The relationship goes public; rivals and friends react.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A claim makes the relationship public. A soldier in a romantic relationship with the commander feels passed over; a close friend or a soldier who values the group respects the gesture; the rest do not care. Refusing her in front of the squad hurts her badly and is only possible when public humiliation is switched on and is not one of her own limits.

short: A keepsake a close soldier gives the commander, once. The commander may wear two: they please the giver and others take note.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A soldier who is close to the commander offers one token, once. Accepted, it is kept; worn, it earns her a little Affinity every day and the others react: a rival is stung, a friend takes note. Taking it off is an offense to her, and a token won in a wager is locked for a week: taking it off early also breaks a promise.

short: A bet between the commander and a soldier: a game and a stake. The result is the dice's, not a social check, and each side wins its own stake.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A soldier with a will of her own challenges the commander, or the commander challenges her. Five games: a coin, rock-paper-scissors, high card, a sparring bout on the combat rules with a handicap she allows, and a bet on the next run. The stakes are a day of obedience, a slot, a privilege, her demand, a token, a truthful answer and, if switched on, her mark. A stake whose category is off is never offered.

short: The loser of a wager follows the winner for the rest of the day, outside combat. Choosing against her pick counts as overriding her.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: When the commander loses, the day goes her way: her pick is pre-selected in her demand, her proposal, a decision and a squad vote, and choosing otherwise costs Trust and Affinity and raises her Impunity. When she loses she follows the commander's non-combat orders: she refuses nothing, asks for nothing and takes nothing on her own initiative. Activities, upgrades and expeditions are never affected.

short: Something the squad keeps from the commander. It comes out by Insight, a slip or a confession; the commander confronts, pretends not to know, or uses it.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A soldier hides a bad injury after a run, the squad strikes a deal on the road, or settles on who would take over. Everyone who knows it is told not to reveal it. When it comes out the commander chooses: confront everyone (every soldier who knew it is put back in line and the whole squad grows cooler), pretend not to know (nothing changes, and the commander alone remembers it) or use it (for two weeks the soldiers who knew it are less sure of themselves). A secret that has not come out cannot be read here.

short: What the squad remembers of what happens to it: facts, a dossier per soldier, a short chronicle and her story with the commander, told to the story model.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Runs, votes, refusals, blame, deaths and what the soldiers do to each other become facts that only the people who were there know. The rest of the squad hears of them later as [[squad_rumor|rumors]]. Old facts are folded into a [[dossier]] instead of being deleted. How much is kept, and how many tokens of every prompt it may use, is set in the settings tab ([[memory_preset|preset]], [[memory_budget|budget]]). Private things never reach a scene with a third soldier present.

short: How much the squad remembers: short, normal or long. Custom lets you set every number once the edit lock is off.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A preset sets how many facts are kept before old ones are folded into a [[dossier]], how many are told to the story model, how many days of the chronicle and how many lines of a soldier's story with the commander reach a prompt, and how many tokens that may use ([[memory_budget|budget]]). Changing the preset never deletes anything by itself.

short: The share of the story prompt that is kept for memory. It never takes the room of the scene header or of the soldiers present.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The prompt has one token cap. Memory gets a guaranteed part of it; what memory does not use goes back to everything else. If the budget is more than half of the cap the settings tab warns you, because the rest of the prompt has to fit in what is left. A line that does not fit is cut, the least important first.

short: How full the squad's memory is: facts kept, dossiers, chronicle entries, the tokens the last prompt used and the size of the save.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: When the facts pass the limit of the preset, the oldest are folded into dossiers one soldier at a time; only if that cannot run are the least important ones deleted, past a quarter more than the limit. Pinned facts are counted apart and are never folded or deleted. A hidden fact is not counted here.

short: Two short paragraphs about a soldier (or the squad as a whole) that replace her old facts: what only she and the commander know, and what everyone knows.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: When a soldier has many old facts they are folded into her dossier by the mechanic model (or joined and cut if there is none). The squad's part is told in every scene she is in; her private part only in a private scene with her or in a message to her. You can read the dossier in her file and, with the edit lock off, edit it.

short: What happened to some of the squad is heard by the rest within a few days. A soldier who only heard of it knows it as hearsay.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A fact that the squad should hear of spreads at day end: fast (two days) or slow (four), faster when it matters a lot. The days are fixed by the save, not rolled. In a scene a soldier who only heard of it is told it is a rumor. With the rumor setting on the mechanic model may retell it in the voice of whoever tells it.

short: A fact you keep: it is never folded or deleted and it counts more when the story model picks what to remember.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Pin a fact in a soldier's memory view. A pinned fact stays in the list however old it gets and is more likely to be told in a scene. You can forget any fact; with the edit lock off you can also rewrite it.

short: Optionally the chat messages of scenes that are long over are hidden from the story model, once they have been summarized. They stay in the chat for you.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Set a number N in the settings tab: the messages of every ended scene older than the last N scenes are hidden from the model (SillyTavern's hide). A scene whose summary failed is never hidden. Turn it back to 0 and exactly the messages Alius hid are shown again; lines SillyTavern or other tools hid are left as they are.

short: The squad's biotelemetry: a live line for each named soldier's pulse and temperature, reported by her implant.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Vitals show a pattern (steady, elevated, spiking, flat or erratic) and two readings in bands, never exact figures. The pattern follows her stress and what has just happened: a fight, a quarrel, the commander near, an unmet desire. It says that something moves her, not what she feels.

short: A line that barely moves whatever happens. It is how a dampened soldier reads; it is not calm.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A soldier whose emotions are dampened by a fault keeps a flat line even in a fight or a quarrel. Only a rare flicker breaks it, and a flicker is a logged moment: something reached her.

short: A moment when a flat line broke. It is logged with its day and slot.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A flicker is written down when warmth or interest toward the commander rises sharply in a soldier whose line is otherwise flat. The log lists the day and slot only; what happened is in the log of the day and in her dossier.

short: How a soldier's messages arrive: hesitation, a deleted line, a double text, a late hour, a voice message, a curt answer.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The game decides these from her state, around the text the model writes: a soldier who is close or wants company may send several short messages; one who is cold answers in a word or two. They are fixed when a message arrives, so an old message never changes. A habit is a sign, not a statement of what she feels.

short: Whether she has read your message, and how many slots ago. Seen with no reply is a choice she made.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The game keeps no clock, so receipts count slots, not hours: READ, READ with the slots since, or SEEN with no reply when she read it and answered nothing. Silence can mean she is busy, hurt or undecided.

short: A message she recorded instead of typing. Play it to read what she said.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Someone close sometimes sends a voice message. The words stay hidden behind the waveform until the commander plays it, and they stay shown until the COMMS view is drawn again.

short: At night the interface turns dimmer and warmer, moves slower and makes less noise. Visitors come to the door.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: While the slot is Night the whole shell shifts to a dim, warm variant of its palette, transitions run slower and sounds play at half their volume. Readable mode keeps the label and the quieter sound but not the dimming. Visits that are not a confrontation arrive as a [[night_door|knock at the door]].

short: A night visit that is not a confrontation. Open, say one thing through the door, or stay silent; the timer counts as silence.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Someone is at the door. [ OPEN ] starts a scene. You may say one line through the door and she answers once, still deciding whether to stay; then only open or silence remain. Staying silent, or letting the timer run out, is a choice with the consequences of an ignored knock, and she may leave a note under the door.

short: Seconds a night knock waits for an answer, 0 to 60. At 0 the door never times out. The default is 15.
long: The countdown is real time. It stops while you type through the door, while she answers, while the analysis panel or a dialog is open and while the page is hidden. When it reaches 0 it counts as staying silent.

short: A model call gave nothing usable. The chip says why; RETRY runs it again, the menu offers a bigger budget or the other model, DROP gives it up.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Every place that asks a model for something (a reading of a conversation, a summary, a decision's wording, an answer by message) can fail. The game never hides it: a chip appears where the answer was due, with the reason in plain words. Where a fallback exists (a plain line for a scene, the authored text of a decision) it already stands, and a later answer replaces it where that is allowed.

short: Ask the model again for what it already gave. It works while nothing depends on the old answer; otherwise the button stays off and says why.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A text can simply be replaced. A decision's wording can be replaced until it is answered. A reading of a conversation or a summary changed the world, so the world is first put back as it was, and only while nothing else has happened since. A reroll costs a call like any other and can fail like any other.

short: What the game keeps of a failed call: who asked, why it failed, the tries and when. Never the prompt, the chat or the model's words. At most 20.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A record closes when its call finally works, when it is dropped or when the fallback is kept. One whose moment has passed (the scene is over, the decision was made) stays listed for the rest of that day and the next, saying why, and then goes. Background work that nobody is waiting for shows in SYS only and does not count on the badge.

short: Refused, cut off, timed out, the connection failed, the answer did not fit the form, nothing came back, or no mechanic profile is selected.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A refusal is never retried on its own (the model would refuse again): pick another model or change what is asked. A cut-off or malformed answer is retried with a bigger budget, a lost connection, a timeout or an empty answer with the same one; how many automatic tries there are is a setting.

short: Seconds a model call may run before it counts as failed, 10 to 600. The default is 120.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A call that has not answered by then is abandoned and shown as a failure with a RETRY. A main-model call cannot be canceled in SillyTavern, so an answer that arrives late is ignored and only logged in debug mode. A slow model needs a longer timeout, not a bigger budget.

short: How many times a failed model call is tried again on its own before the failure is shown, 0 to 2. The default is 1.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A cut-off or malformed answer is retried with a larger budget (x1.5 each time); a lost connection, a timeout or an empty answer with the same budget. A refusal is never retried: the model would refuse again, so it is shown at once and you pick what to change.

short: Each named soldier writes her notes in her own hand. You can change which of the six hands she uses.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A note left in the quarters, in the gear or under the door is written in the soldier's hand. Every soldier starts with a hand picked from her name; the HAND select in her dossier changes it. Readable mode shows notes in the plain type font.

short: The room a soldier lives in. Her quarters scenes show it, and you can change which of the fourteen rooms is hers.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Every named soldier starts in a room picked from her name: cozy, tidy, severe, Japanese, gilded and so on. The QUARTERS select in her dossier changes it. The room is only what you see and how the scene describes it; it changes nothing else.

short: Every soldier has her own cabin on the upper floor, marked with her name. At night and when confined she is there.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Cabins are handed out in the order soldiers joined the unit, scattered over the floor. The first ten never move; the cabin of a soldier who left stays vacant until the turn comes round to it, and a soldier who joined after every cabin was taken may move into one when it frees up. Grunts take whatever cabins are free. Click a cabin to see who is in it and talk to her there.

short: The outpost has a ground floor, an upper floor and the roofs. Switch with 1F / 2F / ROOF, a staircase or PageUp and PageDown.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The ground floor is where the outpost works: the mess, the medbay, the workshop, the garage and the yard. The upper floor is where it lives: the cabins, comms and the commander's cabin. The roof is reached only by the back stairs. Each floor button says how many soldiers are on it.

short: A ring with a C and a diamond: where the commander is when she is not in her own cabin.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The commander is not drawn in her own cabin. When a reason moves her she shows up in the room she is in. Today the one reason is a second place: a soldier who holds the household has her quarters as the commander's second place, and on an evening she booked, the commander is in her cabin.

short: A dark, hatched room is part of the outpost but nothing happens there yet.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Showers, storage, the laundry, the briefing room and the others are drawn so the outpost is whole. They open when a later update gives them something to do.

short: A note a soldier leaves for the commander: in the quarters, in the gear or under the door, in her own hand.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Soldiers who are close leave notes. Quarters notes wait on the desk when the commander comes in, gear notes are tucked into the inventory and door notes are pushed under the door after an unanswered knock. A note lasts a few days, and unread ones raise a badge on HOME.

short: A rule a soldier set, written as a note she signed. Sign it, negotiate it or refuse to sign. A broken rule tears the note.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A close soldier may propose a rule for the relationship. It arrives as her signed note: [ SIGN ] accepts it, [ NEGOTIATE ] asks for terms and [ DON'T SIGN ] refuses. An active rule carries both signatures. When it is broken the note shows torn for a day.

short: What a soldier leaves on the commander's PDA: a sticker on the casing, her picture as the wallpaper, a renamed contact.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A soldier with enough access marks the device as hers. Her sticker sits on the frame, her portrait is the wallpaper on HOME and she may rename her contact in COMMS. Peeling a mark off is an act the soldier notices, so it asks first. After a break-up her marks fade for a week.

short: A campaign premise, chosen at setup: one per campaign. It changes how the whole run is played, not how strong the commander is.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A special trait is not a modifier. It adds a system of its own: a frequency in the commander's head, a mind marked by the Bloom, or a debt to a rival corporation. Each shows a WHAT THIS CHANGES list on its card. Only one can be taken, and the choice cannot be changed after the commander file is reviewed.

short: A fragment of a soldier's thoughts the frequency picked up. It may be true, distorted or only half there; it is never marked.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The analyzer in the commander's head catches fragments in scenes and messages. A fragment can be about a stance, a demand, a warning, a secret or a feeling. Some are distorted, some name only the subject. Nothing tells which; acting on one can give the commander away.

short: The mechanic model words each frequency fragment as a broken thought; off, a template is used.
long: When on, each fragment is worded by the mechanic model in one call. When off, or when the model fails, a template line is used instead. The fragment's truth never depends on the wording.

short: How far a soldier suspects the commander of hearing thoughts. It stays unseen until one of them reacts.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Each time the commander acts on something only the frequency could have told, the soldier it was about grows more suspicious; it fades with time. Some defects make a soldier notice sooner. At the top she is sure, and she tells others.

short: The commander said or did something only a frequency fragment could have told. The soldier it was about notices.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A leak is read from the conversation, not rolled: if the commander acts on an intercepted fragment in front of the soldier it was about, her suspicion rises. A false fragment still raises it, a little less, so suspicion never betrays truth.

short: A one-way medbay procedure: the frequency stops for good, and a later discovery lands softer.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Burning the implant ends every fragment, now and later. Suspicion still fades, and a soldier who finds out afterwards reacts less badly, most of all one who hates lies. It cannot be undone.

short: The commander's own strain. Nightmares, a false alarm acted on and a fall in combat raise it; sleep, time and the medbay ease it.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Stress runs from calm to breaking. From strained on, the commander reads people worse: Empathy counts one rank lower. It eases a little every day, more after a night slept through and with a medbay session.

short: A combat order only a paranoid commander has: name a cover who takes the first hit from a unit that turns on the commander.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Contingency costs 2 CP and can be set once per combat. If a mutineer, or a soldier in breakdown, hits the commander, the cover takes that first hit instead. It does nothing against ordinary enemies.

short: An early warning that a soldier may doubt, desert, mutiny or defy. It reaches the commander a day or two before it shows.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: A premonition is a notice, not a fact. Some are real and arrive before the soldier's own sign; some are false alarms that look exactly the same. Acting on a real one can head it off. Acting on a false one is an insult or a coercion with full consequences.

short: A premonition about a soldier who is planning nothing. It looks exactly like a real one.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Each day a premonition may come with nothing behind it; a sharper Insight makes it rarer, and a bad night makes it likelier. Accusing, punishing, benching or using the Leash on a soldier on a false alarm costs trust, adds commander stress and is remembered.

short: A night of Bloom dreams: commander stress goes up, the next morning may be lost, and a fond soldier may come to the door.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Nightmares come more often when the commander is already strained. After one, false alarms are likelier for a day.

short: A contact from a rival corporation who buys the commander's intel at night, about once a week. The squad never meets one.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: The handler comes to the gate, not to a soldier's door. For each piece of intel the commander answers truth, partial, false or withhold. Truth pays and comes back as trouble; withholding makes the handler press harder.

short: What the commander sells the handler: for each item, truth, partial, false or withhold. Truth pays and comes back as trouble.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Each visit offers up to five pieces of recent intel. Truth pays in full and later returns as an ambush, sabotage or a shift in standing; partial pays half and hurts less; false pays and costs nothing at first but may be found out; withholding pays nothing and makes the handler press.

short: How hard the handler is pressing: calm, pressing or threatening. Withholding raises it, truth lowers it.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Pressure and the handler's suspicion of false intel decide what the handler does: first a threat, then a cut payment, and finally a leak of the commander's crime to the whole squad.

short: An unseen threat: how close the corporation's own oversight is to tracing a leak back to the commander.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Each consequence of sold intel that lands adds to it. Cunning slows it and a brutal oversight speeds it. At the top oversight finds out and the commander must decide what to do.

short: The storyline that opens when the dealings with the rival corporation come out: become a double agent, confess, or flee.
long: AUTHOR TO WRITE: Each of the three ends has its own cost. The arc stays open afterwards; its beats are the author's.

short: A campaign mode in which the commander carries the controller implant and one soldier holds the Leash.
long: In LEASHSWAP the commander is under the Leash like the squad. One soldier, the [[warden]], holds the controller for the corporation: she expects things of the commander, can override orders and can punish. The mode is chosen at setup, and what happens when the commander dies is set by the [[death_rule]].

short: The soldier who holds the commander's controller for the corporation.
long: The warden is one soldier of the squad. She has an agenda of expectations, can override the commander's orders and can punish. She is outside the squad's hierarchy: she sits above it. She is picked at setup, by you or by the corporation (the unit most loyal to it).

short: What happens when the commander dies: the day is rewound, or the campaign ends.
long: Chosen at setup and fixed for the campaign. REWIND DAY restores the start of the day and hides the scenes played since, so the death leaves no memory. CAMPAIGN END closes the campaign, writes an epilogue from the chronicle and makes the save read-only. The default follows the combat difficulty: Story and Normal rewind the day, Hard ends the campaign.

short: Something the warden expects of the commander. She judges every order against what she expects.
long: The warden's agenda holds three to five expectations, each with a weight. You see only the ones you have learned: from an override that names one, from what she says and does, or from digging. The rest show as unknown. An order that cuts across an expectation may be overridden, and the heavier the expectation, the likelier the override.

short: The mechanic model judges whether an order cuts across one of the warden's personal expectations. Off, only the engine's rules count.
long: Costs one very short model call before an out-of-combat order while the warden has a personal expectation. The model only names which expectation an order touches and how much; the engine decides whether she overrides. Combat never calls it.

short: What the warden does to the commander after open defiance: a reprimand, lost privileges, confinement, humiliation, pain or the Leash.
long: After a defiance the warden may punish. The harder the defiance, the harder the punishment: it follows how much open disobedience has built up. A punishment deters (it lowers defiance) and satisfies her. The Leash on the commander is the hardest and needs one of her weekly authorizations.

short: The warden can use the controller on the commander: compel forces the next choice, suppress takes the rest of the day.
long: The warden has a few Leash authorizations a week from oversight, refilled with the squad's. Compel means the next override can only be answered COMPLY, and a major decision becomes hers. Suppress takes the rest of the day and leaves the commander shaken. Using one is her hardest punishment.

short: A Leash request on a soldier goes through the warden first: she co-signs or denies it.
long: While a warden holds the Leash, every request to compel, suppress or terminate a soldier needs her co-sign. A denial spends no authorization, is logged with her name and leaves the situation as it was. Her answer depends on how satisfied she is and on her own mind; a request against the warden herself is always denied.

short: How much open disobedience the warden has seen. It fades by itself, and she answers it.
long: Defiance rises when the commander defies an override or breaks what she expects, and it fades a little every day. Crossing 50 earns a warning, 75 a final warning. Only after two warnings on two different days can it end in the controller being triggered. A punishment lowers it, and complying does too.

short: Two warnings on different days come before the controller is triggered. Then the death rule decides what happens.
long: At 50 defiance the warden warns the commander; at 75 she gives the final warning, but never on the same day as the first. At 100, with two warnings behind, the controller is triggered and the commander is dead. What follows is set by the death rule chosen at setup: the day is rewound, or the campaign ends. Being downed in combat is an injury, not this.

short: The warden countermands an order that cuts across what she expects. Answer: COMPLY, ARGUE or DEFY.
long: When an order conflicts with one of her expectations, she may stop it: nothing happens and no slot is spent. COMPLY does what she wants instead. ARGUE opens a scene: only a real compromise runs the commander's order with no price; in a fight it is one roll. DEFY runs the commander's order, raises her defiance, lowers her satisfaction and may earn a punishment. While the commander is compelled only COMPLY is open.

short: How content the warden is with the commander. The lower it is, the more likely she is to override.
long: Satisfaction rises when the commander complies, keeps what she expects and takes the punishments she gives; it falls when the commander defies her or breaks what she expects. It also decides how readily she co-signs the squad's Leash requests. You see it as a band, never as a number, unless raw values are on.

short: Quiet moves against the warden: win allies, dig for kompromat, open the implant. Each one is noise, and noise gets noticed.
long: Allies are won in conversation, away from the warden. Digging and the implant hack are slot actions. Every move makes noise, and the more noise there is the likelier she finds out. When she does, her trust in the commander crashes, defiance rises, and she punishes at once. The size of the danger is not shown: the panel says only that a threat is unseen.

short: Facts about the warden that the commander holds against her. Three of them are enough to hand her to oversight.
long: A dig turns up something she hid, or something the squad knows. Each fact is kept, tagged and pinned. Digging needs an ally to help or a sharp enough Cunning, takes one slot, and adds noise.

short: A project in three steps to silence the controller. It needs a workshop, a medbay, PLYX and an ally who knows implants.
long: Each step pays PLYX, takes a slot and adds noise. A step that is noticed fails: the progress starts over, the commander takes a pain burst, and the warden learns what is going on. The third clean step makes the controller dark. That removes the warden, and oversight opens an investigation.

short: Oversight opens one when the warden is gone. A clock fills a segment a day, and then comes a verdict.
long: Whatever the route, oversight looks into the warden's removal. Hack is the longest and quietest, her death the shortest and the loudest. Until the clock fills, the controller runs under remote control. What the investigation will find is not shown: the panel says only that a threat is unseen.

short: While the investigation is open oversight runs the controller: quota and obedience, automatic punishments, no negotiation.
long: There is no warden to argue with. A mission failed costs a pain burst, a week with no mission completed costs a reprimand, and defiance does not move because there is no one to defy. Orders are not countermanded.

short: When the investigation closes, the commander is cleared or convicted.
long: Cleared: the commander is free, the implant is dormant and oversight keeps watch. Convicted: oversight assigns a new warden from the squad, and with no one left to hold the Leash the commander is executed and the campaign ends, whatever the death rule says.

short: The campaign begins as if the commander had already been at the base for a while: acquaintance only, no missions or time skipped.
This soldier arrives on day 1 and meets the commander for the first time, even in a head start.
